sentences: The pedagogical value of the exercise was clear to everyone except the students doing it.
Pedagogical fashions change every decade and the chalk stays the same.

pedagogue.definition: a teacher, often a pedantic one
sentences: The pedagogue corrected pronunciation with a relish nobody had asked for.
A pedagogue in Athens was the slave who walked the child to school.

pedagogy.definition: the theory and practice of teaching
sentences: The new pedagogy required smaller classes, which is why it was never adopted.
Good pedagogy is mostly knowing what the learner already believes.
His pedantic correction of the date was, annoyingly, correct and irrelevant.
There is a fine line between pedantic and precise, and it moves depending on who is right.

peddle.definition: to sell or promote, often dubiously
sentences: The consultancy peddled the same slide deck to four competing firms.
He peddled a theory that had been refuted before he was born.
The prose is pedestrian and the argument is brilliant, which is an unusual combination.
A pedestrian performance of a difficult piece is still an achievement, just not a memorable one.
A peevish note about the coffee machine ran to four hundred words.
He grows peevish after nine at night and reasonable again by breakfast.
The word began as a technical term and became purely pejorative within a decade.
Calling something "academic" in a pejorative sense annoys academics enormously.
Her pellucid explanation of the tax change was reprinted in three papers.
The pellucid water made the lake look four feet deep and it was twelve.
He had a penchant for hiring people who disagreed with him, which is rarer than it sounds.
Her penchant for punctuality made everyone else look casual.
The pendulous branches of the willow swept the surface of the pond.
Pendulous shares a root with pendulum, and both are about hanging.
He looked penitent for the duration of the hearing and no longer.
A penitent apology names the harm and offers no explanation.
He grew pensive on the drive home and said nothing for forty miles.
Pensive comes from the French for thinking, with the melancholy included free.
The penultimate chapter is the best and the last one apologizes for it.
People use penultimate to mean very last, which is exactly wrong.

penumbra.definition: a partial shadow; a marginal area
sentences: The right exists in the penumbra of two clauses and has been argued about ever since.
During the eclipse the penumbra dims the light without darkening the sky.
A penurious childhood shaped a lifetime of turning off unused lights.
The penurious offer was withdrawn and replaced with a penurious one.
He wrote four masterpieces in penury and one bad play in comfort.
Penury is poverty without the possibility of a plan.

peon.definition: a lowly worker doing menial tasks
sentences: He described himself as a peon and ran the entire scheduling system.
The peons in the org chart are the ones who know where everything is.

perceive.definition: to become aware of or interpret
sentences: Nobody perceived the pattern until it was plotted rather than tabulated.
How the policy is perceived matters more, politically, than what it does.
A percipient reader will notice the second narrator before the book announces one.
The most percipient question of the evening came from the back row.

peregrinate.definition: to travel about, especially on foot
sentences: They peregrinated across three countries with one map and no plan.
The peregrine falcon is named for wandering, which it does spectacularly.

peremptory.definition: insisting on obedience; allowing no refusal
sentences: A peremptory summons at nine in the morning is never good news.
In law, a peremptory challenge needs no reason at all.

perennial.definition: lasting or recurring year after year
sentences: Parking is the perennial complaint at every meeting in every organization.
Perennial plants come back; annuals require a decision each spring.
The perfidious ally signed two treaties in the same month with opposite parties.
Perfidious Albion was a French insult that the English rather enjoyed.
The perfidy was not the leak but the pretense of outrage about it.
Perfidy requires trust first, which is why strangers cannot commit it.

perfunctory.definition: done without care as a formality
sentences: The perfunctory inspection took nine minutes and missed the entire problem.
A perfunctory apology is worse than none, because it uses up the occasion.
The perilous descent was made twice a day by people carrying water.
Perilous financial ground is easiest to see from the other side of it.
A peripatetic career took him to nine cities and one very tolerant family.
Aristotle taught while walking, which is why the word means wandering.

peripheral.definition: of minor importance; on the edge
sentences: The issue was peripheral to the case and consumed most of the hearing.
Peripheral vision catches motion the center of the eye misses entirely.
The manuscript perished in a fire that spared the far less interesting ledgers.
Publish or perish is the academic slogan that produced a great deal of publishing.
The perjury charge was easier to prove than the crime it concealed.
People rarely go to prison for the offense; they go for the perjury afterward.
The smell of the chip shop permeated three floors of the building.
A culture of caution permeated the department until nobody would sign anything.
The most pernicious myths are the ones that are almost true.
A pernicious habit does no damage in any single instance.

peroration.definition: the grand concluding part of a speech
sentences: The peroration lasted eleven minutes and the argument had ended twenty earlier.
A good peroration makes people forget the middle of the speech, which is often the point.

perpetrate.definition: to carry out a wrong or crime
sentences: The fraud was perpetrated over eleven years by someone universally described as reliable.
Perpetrate is for crimes and, occasionally, for puns.
The perpetual roadworks became a landmark in their own right.
A perpetual motion machine is the physicist's shorthand for a hopeless idea.
The reform perpetuated the very inequality it had been designed to remove.
Retelling the myth perpetuates it; correcting it spreads it further.

perquisite.definition: a benefit attached to a position
sentences: The perquisites of the office included a car, a flat, and remarkably little authority.
Perquisite is the full word behind the shorter, cheerier "perk."
Perseverance published the paper that four rejections had nearly killed.
Perseverance is talent's least glamorous and most reliable substitute.
The fault persisted through two replacements and one exorcism attempt.
She persisted with a line of questioning everyone else had abandoned.
A personable candidate with a thin record beat a difficult one with a strong one.
Being personable is a skill and is usually described as a personality.
Her perspicacious reading of the accounts found in a day what auditors missed in a month.
The most perspicacious member of the board was the one who said the least.
His perspicacity about people was matched by total blindness about himself.
Perspicacity is seeing through; perspicuity is being seen through clearly.

perspicuous.definition: clearly expressed and easy to understand
sentences: The judge's perspicuous summary made a complicated case teachable.
Perspicuous writing is rarer than perspicacious thinking.
A pert reply from the junior clerk ended the meeting on a better note.
Pert once meant simply lively and picked up the cheek along the way.
The pertinacious journalist filed the same request eleven times and finally got the file.
Pertinacious is dogged with a slightly disapproving tone.

pertinent.definition: relevant to the matter at hand
sentences: Only one of the forty slides contained anything pertinent.
A pertinent question early saves an impertinent argument later.
The discrepancy perturbed him enough to recount everything by hand.
In physics, to perturb a system is to nudge it and see what it does.
He perused the contract for two hours and found the clause on page nine.
Peruse means to read thoroughly, though half the world now uses it for skimming.
A quiet dread pervaded the office in the week before the announcement.
Damp pervades an old house the way rumor pervades a small firm.
The assumption was so pervasive that nobody thought to write it down.
Pervasive surveillance is noticed only when it fails.
The petulant response to a mild question told everyone what was going on.
Petulant at forty is much less charming than petulant at four.

phalanx.definition: a tightly packed group moving together
sentences: A phalanx of lawyers arrived and the conversation became considerably more expensive.
The Macedonian phalanx worked until somebody found ground it could not cross.
The film's phantasmagorical second half loses half the audience and keeps the other half forever.
A phantasmagoria was a nineteenth-century magic lantern show designed to terrify.
The phenomena were catalogued for eighty years before anyone explained them.
Phenomena is plural; one phenomenon, however striking, is not phenomena.

philanthropist.definition: one who gives generously to good causes
sentences: The philanthropist funded the hospital wing and named it after the disease.
A philanthropist is a rich person whose giving outlives their reputation for getting.

philanthropy.definition: generous giving for the public good
sentences: Nineteenth-century philanthropy built libraries that public funding has struggled to keep open.
Philanthropy is love of humankind, according to the Greek, and tax planning according to the accountant.

philistine.definition: someone hostile to art and culture
sentences: He called them philistines for preferring the sequel and they called him worse.
Philistine as an insult was invented by German students about townspeople.

philology.definition: the study of language in historical texts
sentences: Philology reconstructed a language nobody had spoken for three thousand years.
Tolkien was a philologist first and invented the languages before the stories.

philosophical.definition: calm in the face of difficulty; relating to philosophy
sentences: He was philosophical about the rejection, which took about four days to achieve.
The dispute was philosophical, meaning no experiment would ever end it.
The phlegmatic goalkeeper conceded four and shrugged at every one.
Phlegmatic is one of the four humors, and the only one that sounds like a compliment for a pilot.
The phony credentials were checked, for the first time, in year nine.
A phony apology has the shape of contrition and none of the content.
The picayune objections delayed a decision worth several million.
A picayune was a small coin, which is where the smallness comes from.
Public piety and private conduct diverged sharply, as the letters revealed.
Filial piety in the classic texts outranks almost every other obligation.
Someone had been pilfering stationery for years, and the audit cost more than the pens.
Pilfering is theft that everyone commits and nobody names.

pillage.definition: to rob violently, especially in war
sentences: The city was pillaged twice in a decade and rebuilt each time on the same street plan.
The archive was pillaged politely, by scholars, over two centuries.
He was pilloried in the press for a remark that the transcript did not support.
The pillory was a wooden frame for public humiliation, which the internet has efficiently replaced.
He pined for a city he had left voluntarily and could return to any weekend.
Dogs pine, and so do people, and both look equally foolish about it.

pinion.definition: to restrain by binding the arms
sentences: He was pinioned by two stewards before he reached the stage.
Pinion means the wing joint, and to pinion a bird is to stop it flying.
She reached the pinnacle of the profession and found the view mostly administrative.
The pinnacle of the season was a match nobody had expected them to survive.
Pious hopes about the deadline were expressed by everyone and believed by none.
The pious tone of the memo did nothing to conceal what it was actually asking for.

piquant.definition: pleasantly sharp in taste or interest
sentences: A piquant detail in the third paragraph is what made the story travel.
The sauce was piquant enough to be interesting and mild enough to finish.
He resigned in a fit of pique and asked for the job back within a fortnight.
As a verb it means to arouse: a detail can pique your curiosity and your pride.
The pith of the argument fits in a sentence and took forty pages to reach.
Pith is the spongy center of a stem, which is the metaphor exactly.
Her pithy summary was quoted more often than the report it summarized.
Pithy takes longer to write than rambling, which is why rambling is more common.

pittance.definition: a very small amount of money
sentences: He was paid a pittance for a design that made somebody else a fortune.
The fund's entire budget was a pittance beside the problem it addressed.
The refund placated most of them and infuriated the ones who had not asked.
Trying to placate both factions produced a statement that pleased neither.

placebo.definition: an inert treatment given as if real
sentences: The placebo group improved by eleven percent, which is medicine's most humbling fact.
The whole scheme was a placebo: it changed how people felt and nothing else.
The placid surface of the meeting concealed four separate resignations in progress.
A placid temperament is worth more in a crisis than any amount of expertise.
A plaintive email arrived at midnight asking whether anyone had read the draft.
The plaintive call of the curlew is the sound of that entire coastline.
The young brain is remarkably plastic, which is both a gift and a warning.
A plastic personality adapts to every room and is trusted in none.

plasticity.definition: the ability to be shaped or adapt
sentences: Neural plasticity explains why the stroke patient recovered speech in eleven months.
The plasticity of the material is what allows the whole design to work.
The speech offered platitudes to a room that had come for a number.
A platitude is a truth that has been repeated until it stopped meaning anything.
The explanation was plausible and, as the receipts showed, entirely invented.
Plausible deniability is a phrase invented by people planning to need it.

plead.definition: to beg earnestly; to argue in court
sentences: She pleaded for one more week and offered to work through the weekend.
He pleaded ignorance, and the emails pleaded otherwise.
His plebeian tastes in music were his most endearing quality.
In Rome, plebeian meant simply not patrician, and the insult came later.
A plenitude of data and a poverty of interpretation described the whole field.
The plenitude of the harvest that year is still spoken about in the village.
A plethora of options made the decision harder rather than better.
Plethora strictly means too many, not simply a lot.
A pliant board approved everything and asked about none of it.
Willow is pliant enough to weave, which is why baskets exist.

plod.definition: to walk or work slowly and laboriously
sentences: He plodded through the dataset for six weeks and found the error everyone else had skipped.
The plot plods for two hundred pages and then, suddenly, sprints.
The plodding investigation succeeded where four brilliant theories had failed.
Plodding is undervalued until the deadline arrives.
The delay was a ploy to run the clock past the funding deadline.
It was a transparent ploy and it worked anyway.

plucky.definition: brave in the face of difficulty
sentences: The plucky underdog lost narrowly and sold considerably more shirts.
Plucky is what the press calls a small team it does not expect to win.

plumb.definition: to explore or measure the depth of
sentences: The report plumbs the causes and skims the remedies.
To plumb a depth was to drop a lead weight, which is where plumbers got their name.
Sales plummeted the week after the recall and never fully recovered.
The temperature plummeted overnight and the pipes announced it by morning.
The location was the one plus in an otherwise dismal listing.
Being underestimated turned out to be a considerable plus.
Critics called it a democracy in form and a plutocracy in funding.
A plutocracy rarely calls itself one, which is part of how it works.

podium.definition: a raised platform for a speaker
sentences: He gripped the podium for ninety minutes and never once looked up.
Strictly, you stand on a podium and behind a lectern, which nobody observes.
The poignancy of the last letter comes from how ordinary it is.
Time adds poignancy to photographs that were dull when taken.
The most poignant detail was the shopping list still on the fridge.
Poignant shares a root with puncture: it pierces.
Her poise during the hostile interview was the reason she got the job.
Poise looks like calm and is usually preparation.

polarize.definition: to divide into sharply opposed groups
sentences: The proposal polarized a committee that had agreed on everything for eleven years.
Nothing polarizes a village like a decision about the church roof.
A polarized debate produces two audiences and no listeners.
The polarized coverage described two entirely different events.

polemic.definition: a strong verbal or written attack
sentences: The book is a polemic and admits it in the first sentence, which is honest.
A polemic is an argument that has chosen a side before starting.
His polemical style sold books and closed doors in equal measure.
The polemical essay is a genre in which nobody has ever changed their mind.

policy.definition: a course of action adopted by an organization
sentences: The policy existed in a document nobody had read since it was written.
Policy is what you do repeatedly, not what the handbook says.

politic.definition: prudent and shrewd in the circumstances
sentences: It was politic to praise the outgoing director and accurate to do neither.
A politic silence at the right moment is worth a paragraph of argument.
A polity of four thousand people ran on volunteers and one paid clerk.
The polity survived a change of religion, two invasions, and a spelling reform.
The pollyannaish forecast assumed nothing would ever go wrong, and things did.
Pollyanna, from the novel, found something to be glad about in every disaster.
The polyglot receptionist handled six languages and one very difficult courier.
A true polyglot dreams, occasionally, in the wrong one.

polymath.definition: someone with expertise in many fields
sentences: The polymath published on optics, poetry, and the drainage of marshes.
Specialization has made polymaths rarer and biographies of them more popular.
The pomp of the opening cost more than the exhibition it opened.
Pomp works precisely because everyone knows it is unnecessary.
The pomposity of the introduction made the modest talk that followed a relief.
Pomposity is the sound of somebody defending a position they suspect is weak.
The pompous email announced a policy that could have been a sentence.
Pompous people are rarely the most senior person in the room.
The ponderous prose of the introduction deters everyone except the examiners.
A ponderous machine is safe and impossible to move.
His pontifical tone about a subject he had read about that week irritated everybody.
Pontifical properly means papal, and everything else about the word is borrowed weight.

pontificate.definition: to speak in a pompous, dogmatic way
sentences: He pontificated about journalism to a table of working journalists.
To pontificate is to speak as though from a throne nobody has offered you.

populist.definition: appealing to ordinary people against elites
sentences: The populist tax cut polled brilliantly and cost the treasury for a decade.
Populist is a description of a strategy, not of a policy's contents.

porous.definition: full of holes; easily passed through
sentences: The border was porous in both directions and policed in only one.
The confidentiality agreement proved porous within a week.

portend.definition: to be a warning sign of
sentences: Falling attendance portended a closure that the board announced two years later.
Comets were believed to portend disaster, which they occasionally coincided with.
The portentous music told the audience to be worried nine seconds too early.
His portentous delivery made a routine announcement sound like a prophecy.

posit.definition: to put forward as a basis for argument
sentences: The paper posits a mechanism and spends thirty pages failing to find it.
Let us posit, for argument, that everyone acted in good faith.
The posthumous award was accepted by a grandson who had never met him.
Posthumous fame is the least useful kind and the most common for poets.

postulate.definition: to assume as true for argument
sentences: Euclid postulated five things and built the whole of geometry on them.
He postulated a cause that no measurement has ever detected.
The local potentate controlled the water and therefore everything else.
He ran the department like a minor potentate, complete with a favored courtier.
A quick powwow in the corridor settled what four emails had not.
The word is borrowed from Algonquian and has drifted a long way from its origin.
In theory the two are identical; in practice they differ by four hours.
Practice does not make perfect; it makes permanent, which is why technique matters.
Practitioners knew the guideline was unworkable a year before the researchers did.
The gap between practitioner and theorist is where most bad policy lives.
The pragmatic solution was ugly, cheap, and still running eleven years later.
Being pragmatic is a virtue until it becomes an excuse.
He prattled through the entire train journey and never once asked a question.
Prattle is talk that requires no listener and rarely notices its absence.

pre-empt.definition: to act first to prevent something
sentences: The announcement pre-empted a leak that was scheduled for the following morning.
She pre-empted the objection by raising it herself in the second paragraph.
After nine minutes of preamble he arrived at a request that took ten seconds.
The preamble to a constitution is where the arguments are hidden.
The company's position was precarious for two years and looked fine in the accounts.
Precarious originally meant held only by someone else's prayer or permission.

preceded.definition: came before in time or order
sentences: A period of silence preceded the announcement, which everybody read correctly.
The symptoms preceded the diagnosis by two years.

precedent.definition: an earlier case used as a guide
sentences: The decision set a precedent nobody intended and everybody later cited.
There was no precedent, which meant everyone invented one and disagreed.
The first precept of the trade was: never sign what you have not read.
Precepts are easy to state and, at three in the morning, hard to follow.
The resignation precipitated a crisis that had been waiting eleven months for an excuse.
Adding acid precipitated a solid, which is where the metaphor comes from.
A precipitous drop in orders was blamed on the weather for two quarters.
The precipitous path down to the beach ends most seasons with an ambulance.
A one-page precis persuaded the minister where a hundred pages had not.
Writing a precis is the fastest way to discover whether you understood the thing.
The precision of the measurement exceeded the accuracy of the assumption behind it.
Precision in language costs a little effort and prevents a great deal of argument.
The clause precluded any appeal, which nobody noticed until an appeal was needed.
Being right does not preclude being unbearable about it.
The precocious student corrected the lecturer, correctly, in the second week.
Precocious means ripening early, and the metaphor includes the warning.
The pamphlet was a precursor to a movement that never credited it.
Every overnight technology has a precursor that failed for want of a battery.

predecessor.definition: the person who held a role before
sentences: He blamed his predecessor for four years and his successor blamed him for five.
Her predecessor left excellent notes, which is rarer than a good handover meeting.
The predicament was of his own making and none the easier for it.
Their predicament had two exits and both required admitting something.
Her predilection for difficult sources produced a book nobody could contradict.
He had a predilection for hiring people from his own college, which the data revealed.
The panel was predisposed to approve and the presentation barely mattered.
Some people are genetically predisposed to the condition and never develop it.

preempt.definition: to take action before someone else can
sentences: The broadcast was preempted by a speech nobody had scheduled.
He preempted the criticism by publishing his own errors first.
A preemptive apology is often more effective than an accurate one.
The preemptive strike was justified afterward with intelligence nobody could produce.

preen.definition: to groom oneself; to show self-satisfaction
sentences: He preened for a week after the mention and forgot who had arranged it.
Birds preen to keep feathers waterproof, which is more useful than the human version.
The whole encounter had been premeditated down to the seating plan.
Premeditation is the difference between a tragedy and a sentence.

premise.definition: an assumption on which an argument rests
sentences: The premise was never stated and never true, which made the argument unfalsifiable.
Attack the premise, not the conclusion; that is where the arguments are won.

prescience.definition: knowledge of events before they happen
sentences: The memo's prescience is remarkable and it was ignored twice.
Prescience in business writing is usually one lucky guess in twenty.
Her prescient warning about the supplier was filed and rediscovered after the collapse.
The novel looks prescient because everything else changed to match it.

presentiment.definition: a feeling that something is about to happen
sentences: She had a presentiment about the flight and took the later one, uneventfully.
Presentiments are remembered when right and forgotten when wrong, which explains their reputation.
The presumption of innocence is easier to state than to observe in a headline.
It was a presumption to answer for the whole department, and he did it anyway.
The presumptive nominee lost the nomination in a way nobody had modeled.
A presumptive diagnosis guides treatment while the tests are still running.
It was presumptuous to announce the appointment before the interview.
Presumptuous is confidence spent on somebody else's territory.
They kept up the pretense of a partnership for eighteen months after it ended.
He abandoned all pretense of impartiality in the second paragraph.
The pretentious menu described a sandwich in forty words.
Calling something pretentious is often a claim about the speaker's own taste.

preternatural.definition: beyond what is natural or normal
sentences: She had a preternatural memory for faces and none at all for names.
The stillness before the storm felt preternatural to everyone on the beach.
Common sense prevailed in the fourth hour of the meeting.
The prevailing wind decides which side of the tree the moss grows on.

prevaricate.definition: to speak evasively to avoid the truth
sentences: He prevaricated for twenty minutes and then admitted it in one sentence.
Prevaricating under oath is a slower route to the same charge.

primacy.definition: the state of being first in importance
sentences: The primacy of safety over schedule was asserted in every document and reversed in practice.
The primacy effect means the first item on a list is the one remembered.
She primed the witness on procedure and nothing else, which is the legal line.
The wall must be primed or the paint will lift within a year.
A principled refusal cost him the contract and won him the next three.
Principled and stubborn look identical from the outside.
The pristine copy sold for eleven times the price of the read one.
The pristine landscape was managed intensively for four hundred years.
His probity was never questioned, which is why the discrepancy was assumed to be an error.
Probity is the quality that makes an audit boring.
The case was lost on a procedural point that had nothing to do with the facts.
Procedural objections are how you delay a decision without opposing it.

proceeding.definition: a formal legal or official process
sentences: Proceedings began in March and concluded, exhausted, in the following December.
The proceedings were published in a volume that four people opened.

proceeds.definition: money obtained from an event or sale
sentences: The proceeds from the auction funded the roof and half the argument about it.
All proceeds go to charity, said the sign, after expenses that consumed most of them.
His proclivity for last-minute changes cost the design team every weekend.
A proclivity is a tendency the speaker slightly disapproves of.
Prodigal spending in the first year left nothing for the second.
The prodigal son wasted the money; the parable is about the welcome, not the waste.

prodigious.definition: impressively great in size or extent
sentences: His prodigious output ran to sixty volumes and one genuinely great book.
A prodigious memory is useful; a selective one is often happier.

prodigy.definition: a person with exceptional early talent
sentences: The prodigy played at eight, burned out at nineteen, and taught happily thereafter.
Being called a prodigy is a burden dressed as a compliment.
Proficient in four languages, he was funny in exactly one.
Proficient is the level at which you stop thinking about the technique.
Profligate use of water in a drought year cost the estate its license.
He was profligate with money and miserly with credit.
The change was profound and took eleven years to become visible.
A profound silence followed a question nobody wanted to answer.
The profundity of the essay is hidden inside a very plain style.
Obscurity is often mistaken for profundity, to the advantage of the obscure.
His profuse apologies took longer than the offense had.
Profuse bleeding is a medical emergency; profuse thanks is merely awkward.
A profusion of wildflowers followed the year the mowing budget was cut.
The profusion of options in the catalogue guaranteed nobody chose anything.
The little machine was the progenitor of an industry worth billions.
Every progenitor of a movement is disowned by its third generation.
Economists prognosticate confidently and revise quietly.
He prognosticated a collapse annually and was eventually, briefly, correct.
The prognostications for the season were wrong in a novel and interesting way.
A prognostication is a guess wearing a suit.

prohibitive.definition: so high as to prevent something
sentences: The prohibitive cost of insurance closed the swimming pool, not the swimming.
The rules were prohibitive in practice and permissive on paper.

project.definition: to estimate for the future; to convey outwardly
sentences: He projected confidence and revised the numbers privately that evening.
Projecting last year's growth for a decade produces a very silly number.

projection.definition: a forecast based on current trends
sentences: The projection assumed no recessions, which is optimistic for a ten-year window.
Every projection is a set of assumptions wearing a number's clothing.
The proletarian novel was praised by critics who had never held a shovel.
Proletarian in Rome meant someone whose only contribution was children.
Committees proliferated until there was one for coordinating the others.
The species proliferated in the absence of anything that would eat it.
A prolific author with one good book is common; the reverse is rarer.
The prolific apple tree fed the whole street and ruined the lawn.
The prolix contract said in nine pages what three would have covered better.
Prolix writing is usually a sign of unfinished thinking.
The prolixity of the introduction cost the paper its only reader.
Prolixity is what happens when nobody is allowed to cut.
The prologue explains a war that the novel then declines to mention again.
This meeting is a prologue; the real decision happens on Thursday.
A promiscuous use of the word "crisis" has left it meaning very little.
Promiscuous citation, where everything supports everything, fools nobody who checks.

promulgate.definition: to make known officially; to spread widely
sentences: The regulation was promulgated in June and enforced, sporadically, from November.
The doctrine was promulgated by pamphlet and spread faster than its author intended.

prone.definition: likely to suffer from; lying face down
sentences: The design was prone to failure in exactly the conditions it was built for.
He is prone to exaggeration, by roughly a factor of three.
There was a pronounced limp that he insisted was a nothing.
The effect was pronounced in one group and invisible in the other.
The error propagated through nine downstream systems before anyone noticed.
Cuttings propagate the plant faster than seed and produce identical copies.
His propensity for optimism made him a poor forecaster and a good manager.
The material has a propensity to crack in exactly the wrong month.
The property that matters here is that it does not conduct heat.
Property in the eighteenth century decided who could vote.
The 1998 memo looks prophetic and was, at the time, merely careful.
Prophetic warnings are recognized only after the thing they warned about.
They propitiated the regulator with a report nobody expected to be read.
Ancient sacrifices were meant to propitiate gods with an interest in weather.
The moment was propitious: cheap money, cheap rent, and no competitors.
He waited for a propitious moment that never arrived and acted anyway.
The chief proponent of the merger left before it completed.
Every proponent of simplicity has a complicated implementation plan.
Questions of propriety delayed the appointment by four months.
Propriety is a rule you notice only when someone breaks it.
The prosaic explanation was correct: somebody had unplugged it to charge a phone.
Prosaic means prose-like, which is an unfair insult to prose.
The organization was proscribed in one country and funded in another.
Prescribe recommends, proscribe forbids, and the two are constantly confused.
